problem.t: Every project starts here: a vague wish becomes a measurable question, **will this customer cancel within 30 days?** The chips that appear will build up into the whole workflow.

data.t: We have **1,000 customer observations over 20 weeks**, with about **20% churn**. Knowing this base rate matters, because it is what any model has to beat.

features-target.t: Five features known on day 0, target **churned_30d**, and the leaky **closed date removed**. Checking for leakage here prevents a falsely perfect model later.

split.t: A **chronological** 700 / 150 / 150 split, made before any results are examined, with the **test set locked**.

baseline.t: A simple rule sets the bar: **0.81 accuracy but recall of only 0.40**. Without a baseline we cannot tell whether a model adds any value.

choose-model.t: A **logistic-style** and a **tree-style** model are chosen as **candidates to test**, not as winners picked in advance.

train.t: Training adjusts **parameters** using the **training data only**, repeating predict, measure the loss, update.

validate.t: On validation data the logistic-style model gets **F1 0.67 and recall 0.70**, which is **below the goal**. The validation set is where we find out what is not good enough yet.

diagnose.t: Compare the train and validation scores. **Poor on both** suggests underfitting, while **0.97 against 0.59** suggests overfitting. The pattern tells us what to try next.

tune.t: Validation picks **max_depth 4** (F1 **0.676**), while the training score alone would have picked 8. Settings are chosen on validation, never on the test set.

compare.t: Under one fair protocol the tree meets the goal, with **recall 0.80 and precision 0.59**. Models are compared against the goal, not just by the highest number.

lock.t: The model and its settings are **locked**: tree-style, max_depth 4. With no more changes allowed, the test result will actually mean something.

final-test.t: The test set is evaluated **once**: **precision 0.54, recall 0.79, F1 0.64**. A little below validation is normal, because validation was used to make choices and the test set was not.

monitor.t: After launch, average usage has shifted by **25%** from training. In this **toy example** we use a 15% tolerance, so we would investigate and possibly retrain. That threshold is a teaching value, not a universal rule.

complete-workflow.t: The yellow arrow shows the loop: diagnosing, tuning and comparing **feed back into choosing a model**. **Remember:** reliable ML is a disciplined, iterative process, not “pick an algorithm, train, done”.
